what_it_does: Quantum computers are prone to errors — individual quantum bits (qubits) can flip unexpectedly due to noise — so quantum error correction codes are used to detect and fix these flips before they corrupt a computation. Decoding the error-correction signals (figuring out which qubits flipped and how to fix them) must happen in real time and must be very accurate. One decoding strategy frames the problem as an Ising model, which is a physics concept where a system settles into a low-energy configuration representing the most likely error pattern — similar to how magnets align. However, existing Ising-based decoders are either slow (high computational complexity) or less accurate than the best-known method (called minimum-weight perfect matching). This paper introduces WRIM, a weighted Ising decoder that uses a geometric region shaped like a polygon to focus the Ising search only on plausible error chains, and tunes the interaction strengths and bias terms to improve both accuracy and speed relative to prior Ising decoders.
